decks.domain: Crash reporting and assisting at a crash, moving vehicles and quick clearance, failure-to-stop penalties, traffic stop safety and the emergency kit

cards.front: If you are in a crash, why should you stay at the scene?
cards.back: If you are in a crash, stay at the scene to help anyone who is injured and to exchange information with the other drivers.

cards.front: What information should you share after a crash?
cards.back: After a crash, share your driver license number, name and address, insurance company and policy number, any witness information and license plate numbers.

cards.front: If anyone is injured in a crash, what must you do?
cards.back: If anyone is injured in the crash, you must call the police immediately.

cards.front: You arrive early at a crash scene. Where do you park, and what lights do you use?
cards.back: When you arrive early at a crash scene, park well off the roadway and switch on your hazard flashers.

cards.front: At a crash scene, what should be done with the ignitions of the vehicles involved?
cards.back: At a crash scene, turn off the ignition of the vehicles involved.

cards.front: At a crash scene, whom should you call?
cards.back: At a crash scene, call nine one one to notify emergency officials.

cards.front: At a crash scene, where should you not stand or walk?
cards.back: At a crash scene, do not stand or walk in the traffic lanes.

cards.front: At a crash scene, what can you ask other people who stopped to do?
cards.back: At a crash scene, ask others who have stopped to warn approaching traffic.

cards.front: How do the duties of an involved driver and a first arrival differ?
cards.back: A driver in a crash calls the police immediately when someone is injured, while a bystander arriving first calls nine one one and warns traffic through others.

decks.module: Moving vehicles after a minor crash
decks.domain: Crash reporting and assisting at a crash, moving vehicles and quick clearance, failure-to-stop penalties, traffic stop safety and the emergency kit

cards.front: When must crashed vehicles be moved off the main roadway?
cards.back: When a crash causes no serious physical injury or death, the vehicles involved must be moved off the main traveled part of the roadway.

cards.front: Who may move a crashed vehicle, and when?
cards.back: Any licensed driver may move a crashed vehicle if it can run under its own power without a tow and moving it will not cause more damage or more traffic hazards.

cards.front: Are you at fault just because you moved your car off the road before police arrived?
cards.back: A person who moves a vehicle off the main roadway before police arrive is not held liable or at fault for the crash just because the vehicle was moved.

cards.front: Does moving your car before police arrive make you liable?
cards.back: Moving your car before police arrive is protected, since the move alone cannot make you liable or at fault for the crash.

cards.front: After a minor crash with no injuries, when should drivers move operable vehicles?
cards.back: After a minor crash with no injuries, drivers should move operable vehicles out of the travel lanes as soon as it is safe.

cards.front: What does state law require after a minor, injury-free crash?
cards.back: State law requires a driver in a minor, injury-free crash to remove the vehicle from the roadway if it can be driven and moved safely.

cards.front: Why get out of the travel lanes after a minor crash?
cards.back: Getting out of the travel lanes gives you a safer place to check for damage, protects first responders and lowers the chance of a secondary crash.

cards.front: When must crashed vehicles be moved off the main roadway?
cards.back: When a crash involves no serious physical injury or death, vehicles must be removed from the main traveled roadway if they remain safely operable under their own power without needing towing and moving them will not cause further vehicle damage or increase traffic hazards.

decks.domain: Crash reporting and assisting at a crash, moving vehicles and quick clearance, failure-to-stop penalties, traffic stop safety and the emergency kit

cards.front: After any crash, what is your first step?
cards.back: After any crash, your first step is to make sure that you and everyone in your vehicle are OK.

cards.front: After a crash, if your vehicle still runs, where should you go?
cards.back: If your vehicle still runs after a crash, move to the emergency shoulder or median or exit the highway, then call nine one one.

cards.front: After a crash, how should you act around traffic?
cards.back: After a crash, stay out of the travel lanes, stay alert and watch the approaching traffic.

cards.front: May you ever leave the scene of a crash?
cards.back: Never leave the scene of a crash.

cards.front: After a crash, may you move to the shoulder, and may you leave the scene?
cards.back: Moving to the shoulder, median or an exit after a crash is expected, but leaving the crash scene altogether is never allowed.

cards.front: In a crash with damage, injury or death, what does the law require?
cards.back: A driver in a crash involving vehicle damage, injury or death is required by law to stop and remain at the scene.

cards.front: At such a crash, what aid must you give?
cards.back: At such a crash you must give aid to anyone injured, including calling nine one one to arrange medical treatment.

cards.front: What must you tell emergency responders and police at such a crash?
cards.back: At such a crash you must tell emergency responders and police your name, your address and your plate number.

cards.front: What follows a conviction for failing to stop at a damage-only crash?
cards.back: A conviction for failing to stop at a crash that caused only vehicle damage suspends your driving privilege for one year.

cards.front: What follows failing to stop at a crash with an injury other than serious injury or death?
cards.back: Failing to stop at a crash that caused an injury other than death or serious physical injury brings a three-year revocation.

cards.front: What follows failing to stop at a crash with serious physical injury?
cards.back: Failing to stop at a crash that caused serious physical injury brings a five-year revocation, not counting any time spent incarcerated.

cards.front: What follows failing to stop at a crash that caused a death?
cards.back: Failing to stop at a crash that caused a death brings a ten-year revocation, not counting any time spent incarcerated.

cards.front: How do the penalties for failing to stop at a damage-only and an injury crash differ?
cards.back: Failing to stop at a damage-only crash brings a one-year suspension, while failing to stop at a crash with injury brings a three-year revocation.

cards.front: How do the penalties for failing to stop at a serious-injury and a fatal crash differ?
cards.back: Failing to stop at a crash with serious physical injury brings a five-year revocation, while a crash with a death brings ten years, and neither counts time spent incarcerated.

decks.domain: Crash reporting and assisting at a crash, moving vehicles and quick clearance, failure-to-stop penalties, traffic stop safety and the emergency kit

cards.front: Who approved the manual's traffic stop guidance?
cards.back: The manual's traffic stop guidance was approved by national groups of motor vehicle administrators and law enforcement leaders.

cards.front: Why does an officer pull a driver over?
cards.back: An officer pulls a driver over when there is reasonable suspicion that a traffic or criminal law was broken.

cards.front: When you see emergency lights behind you, how should you and your passengers act?
cards.back: When you see emergency lights behind you, you and your passengers should stay calm and cooperate.

cards.front: When signaled to stop, how do you pull over?
cards.back: When signaled to stop, use your turn signal and pull off or to the side of the road as soon as it is safe.

cards.front: Once stopped, what should you turn off?
cards.back: Once stopped, turn off the engine and any audio devices.

cards.front: During a traffic stop, should you get out of the vehicle?
cards.back: During a traffic stop, stay in your vehicle unless the officer tells you to get out.

cards.front: If you are pulled over at night, what should you turn on?
cards.back: If you are pulled over at night, turn on your interior lights to help visibility, and expect the officer may use a spotlight.

cards.front: Where should you keep your hands during a traffic stop?
cards.back: Keep your hands on the steering wheel or somewhere the officer can easily see them.

cards.front: Whose instructions should you and your passengers follow?
cards.back: Follow every instruction the officer gives to you or your passengers.

cards.front: Which window should you lower to talk with the officer?
cards.back: The officer may approach either side of the vehicle, so lower the window on that side to talk.

cards.front: When should you tell the officer about a weapon in the vehicle?
cards.back: If there is a weapon in the vehicle, tell the officer at first contact.

cards.front: When should you reach for your license or vehicle documents?
cards.back: Wait for the officer's instructions before reaching for your license or vehicle documents.

cards.front: How do waiting to reach and telling about a weapon fit together?
cards.back: You keep your hands visible and wait for instructions before reaching, but you speak up right away if there is a weapon in the vehicle.

cards.front: What are the rules for staying in and getting out during a stop?
cards.back: During a stop you stay in the vehicle unless told to get out, and if told to get out you keep your hands visible and stand where directed.
cards.memory_hook: stay in; out with hands visible

cards.front: What will the officer typically explain and ask for?
cards.back: The officer will typically explain the reason for the stop and ask for your license, proof of insurance and registration.

cards.front: Your documents are out of reach. What should you do?
cards.back: If your documents are out of reach, tell the officer where they are and wait for an acknowledgment before reaching for them.

cards.front: What should an officer who is not in uniform show you?
cards.back: An officer who is not in uniform should show law enforcement credentials, and if not, you may ask to see them.

cards.front: If the officer asks you to get out, what should you do?
cards.back: If the officer asks you to get out, keep your hands visible and stand where the officer directs.

cards.front: What actions may the officer take at the end of a stop?
cards.back: The officer may give a warning, write a ticket or make an arrest, will typically explain the action, and you may ask if it is not explained.

cards.front: If you disagree with the officer, where should you contest it?
cards.back: If you disagree with the officer, do not argue at the roadside, but contest the decision in court through the proper legal channels.

cards.front: Where is a disagreement with an officer settled?
cards.back: A disagreement with an officer is settled later in court, not by arguing during the stop.

cards.front: Is signing a traffic ticket an admission of guilt?
cards.back: Signing a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt, but refusing to sign one may lead to your arrest.

cards.front: How do signing and refusing to sign a ticket differ?
cards.back: Signing a ticket is not an admission of guilt, while refusing to sign it may lead to arrest.

cards.front: If you believe an officer acted inappropriately, whom should you contact?
cards.back: If you believe an officer acted inappropriately, contact the officer's agency and ask to speak to a supervisor, ideally soon after the stop.

cards.front: Where does a complaint about an officer's conduct go?
cards.back: A complaint about an officer's conduct goes to the officer's agency, where you can ask for a supervisor, ideally soon after the stop.

cards.front: What vehicle information does the ADOT website offer?
cards.back: The ADOT website offers information on titles and registration, temporary and resident registration, vehicle inspections, emissions testing and vehicle insurance.

cards.front: What items might you carry in an emergency kit?
cards.back: Consider carrying an emergency kit with items such as drinking water, a fire extinguisher, a first aid kit, a flashlight, blankets, jumper cables, flares and a spare tire with a jack and lug wrench.

recap_hooks.text: Stay at the scene, exchange information, and call police at once if anyone is injured.

recaps.module: Moving vehicles after a minor crash

recap_hooks.text: With no serious injury or death, move drivable vehicles off the main roadway; moving does not make you liable.
Check everyone first, move to the shoulder if you can, and never leave the scene.
Failing to stop brings one year for damage, three for injury, five for serious injury and ten for a death.
During a stop, stay calm, stay in the vehicle, keep hands visible and wait for instructions before reaching.
Signing a ticket is not admitting guilt, and disagreements are settled in court, not at the roadside.
